questions.q: Name any three opposition parties that contested the first general election (1951-52) and won seats in the Lok Sabha.
questions.a: Communist Party of India (16 seats), Socialist Party (12 seats), Bharatiya Jana Sangh (3 seats). A wrong answer (e.g., naming BJP, Janata Party, or regional parties like DMK/AIADMK) reveals confusion between 1950s parties and their later successors/avataars, and ignorance of the specific parties analysed in nodes 004-007.

questions.q: Explain why the Socialist Party struggled to present itself as an effective alternative after the Congress declared its goal as the 'socialist pattern of society' in 1955 (Avadi session).
questions.a: The Congress co-opted the Socialist Party's core ideological plank, blurring the distinction between them. Socialists faced a dilemma: oppose a Congress now adopting their rhetoric (risking irrelevance) or cooperate (losing distinct identity). This led to splits (Lohia vs. Asoka Mehta). A wrong answer focusing only on electoral mechanics (FPTP) misses the ideological-strategic trap that crippled opposition differentiation — a key NCERT theme.

questions.q: Apply the concept of 'Congress as social and ideological coalition' to explain why opposition parties in the 1950s primarily influenced policy from the 'margins' rather than as direct alternatives.
questions.a: Congress's coalition accommodated diverse ideologies (right, left, centre) internally through factions. Opposition demands (e.g., land reform, planned economy) often found champions within Congress factions, so the ruling party pre-empted opposition issues. Opposition parties thus pressurised factions indirectly. A wrong answer claiming 'opposition was weak because Congress was popular' ignores the structural mechanism (factional balancing) that made Congress absorb opposition space — central to the 'Congress system' thesis.

questions.q: Analyze the significance of the interim cabinet (1947) including Ambedkar and Shyama Prasad Mukherjee, and Nehru inviting Jayaprakash Narayan, for understanding early Congress-opposition relations.
questions.a: It shows the national movement's inclusive legacy translated into post-independence power-sharing: adversaries were respected colleagues. This personal mutual respect allowed principled debate without delegitimising opponents. Its decline later (as competition intensified) explains why opposition space shrank. A wrong answer treating this as mere 'symbolism' misses how shared freedom-struggle capital created a unique democratic culture where opposition was not 'anti-national' — a contrast to many post-colonial states.

questions.q: Evaluate the claim: 'The 1950s opposition parties failed because they won too few seats to matter.'
questions.a: The claim is flawed. NCERT explicitly states their 'token representation' played a 'crucial role in maintaining the democratic character of the system' by: (1) offering sustained principled criticism, (2) checking Congress, (3) preventing anti-democratic resentment, (4) grooming future leaders (e.g., Lohia, Vajpayee, EMS). Success in democracy ≠ seats alone. A wrong answer equating democratic value with seat count reveals a procedural (electoral) rather than substantive (constitutional) understanding of opposition's role — a common board-exam error.

questions.q: Create a one-paragraph argument defending the view that the 'Congress system' (competition within Congress via factions) was a functional substitute for a strong external opposition in the 1950s, using two specific examples from the NCERT text.
questions.a: A strong answer cites: (1) Factions represented ideological spectrum (right-left-centre) so policy debates occurred internally — e.g., land reform debated by Congress factions, not just by Socialists/CPI. (2) Factional balancing prevented authoritarian drift — e.g., Patel's push for disciplined cadre party was resisted by Nehru's coalition approach. A poor answer merely describes factions without showing how they performed opposition's checking function, missing the analytical core of Rajni Kothari's 'Congress system' concept.
